ONE BLOCK WHILE PLAYINGstart—

One block, while playing

Our trained model plays the real game. It has 15 real frames, 311 to 325, and must draw frame 326, which the player made with a tap. We open block 8 (big.blocks[8], counted from 0 as in the notebook) and print every number it touches, for one square: square 164, where the bird is in frame 326. Red is positive, blue is negative, white is near 0. Hover anything to read the exact number.

0

What happens in one game step?

Every frame goes through the model one at a time: [1, 1, 256, 768]. A push stores a finished frame. A draw pass reads what is stored and changes nothing. Below, the real frames we start from, each with its position (the number RoPE uses) and the key that made it.

for frame in 311 … 325: shelf = push(frame) # 15 passes at noise 0.05: k, v of every block are kept picture = pure noise # frame 326 starts here picture = picture + (0.5 − 1.0) · one_pass(picture, t=1.0, shelf) # draw pass 1: reads the shelf, keeps nothing picture = picture + (0.0 − 0.5) · one_pass(picture, t=0.5, shelf) # draw pass 2: reads the shelf, keeps nothing shelf = push(picture) # pass 3: 326 joins the shelf, 311 drops off
1

How does block 8's shelf fill up?

Each push sends one real frame (with noise 0.05) through all 16 blocks. Inside block 8, the frame reads what is already on the shelf plus its own 256 rows, then its own k and v are added to the shelf. The first frame has nothing to read except itself.

k_all = torch.cat([shelf_k[8], own_k[8]], dim=2) # glue along the rows axis: [1, 12, rows, 64] shelf_k[8] = k_all[:, :, -15 * 256:] # keep the newest 15 frames = the last 3,840 rows

After 15 pushes, block 8 holds this. Head 9 of k, on its side: 64 numbers (rows) × 3,840 stored rows (columns), grouped by frame. These keys are stored plain: not yet turned by RoPE.

2

What goes into block 8 in draw pass 1?

Frame 326 starts as pure noise. It went through embed and blocks 0 to 7 (each reading its own shelf), so what reaches block 8 is a table: 256 rows (one per square) × 768 numbers. One more row, c, carries the key (1, a tap) and the noise level (1.0). Row 164, the bird's square, is marked.

x, row 164[768]
c[768]
rows [1, 1, 256, 768] 1 game, 1 frame (the one being drawn), 256 squares, 768 numbers condition [1, 1, 1, 768] one row for the whole frame: key 1 + noise level 1.0 frame number of these 256 rows = 15 (the shelf is 0 … 14)
3

Before attention: each row is scaled and shifted alone

sh1, sc1, g1, sh2, sc2, g2 = block.ada(c).chunk(6, -1) # c → 6 rows of 768 (block 8's own ada) y = block.n1(x) * (1 + sc1) + sh1 # every row: normalise, then the same scale and shift

No row looks at another here. The same 768 numbers of sc1 and sh1 are used for all 256 squares. Row 164, line by line:

4

Square 164 makes its q, k and v

qkv = block.qkv(y) # Linear(768, 2304): each row 768 → 2,304 q, k, v = qkv.view(1, 256, 3, 12, 64).permute(2, 0, 3, 1, 4) # each [1, 12 heads, 256 rows, 64] q, k = block.qn(q), block.kn(k) # RMSNorm per head: fix the length of every 64-number row

One Linear turns the 768 numbers into 2,304. Numbers 0–767 are q, 768–1535 are k, 1536–2303 are v. Each third is cut into 12 heads of 64. Choose a head:

qkv row 164[2304]
q, this head[64]
qn(q)[64]
k, this head[64]
v, this head[64]

q is what square 164 looks for. k is the label it shows to others. v is what it hands over when someone reads it. Its own k and v join the 3,840 shelf rows for this pass only.

5

RoPE: every row is turned by its frame number

frame_number_all_rows = torch.arange(15 + 1).repeat_interleave(256) # 0 ×256, 1 ×256, …, 15 ×256 = 4,096 numbers q_turned = rope(q, frame_number_all_rows[-256:]) # the 256 rows being drawn are frame 15 K_turned = rope(torch.cat([shelf_k[8], k], 2), frame_number_all_rows) # shelf rows 0 … 14, own rows 15

Pair i is number i and number i+32. Each pair is turned by angle = frame number × speed of the pair, with speed = 1000−i/32. Square 164's q is at frame number 15. Four of its 32 pairs, worked out:

qn(q) plain[64]
turn pair i by 15 × speed_i
q turned[64]

The same happens to every k row, each with its own frame number. Below, all 4,096 k rows of this head before and after turning. The plain shelf table is what is stored; the turned one is made fresh in every pass.

6

One score: q times k, number by number

score = (q_turned[164] * K_turned[row]).sum() / 8 # 64 products, added, divided by √64 = 8

Square 164 of the frame being drawn scores four real rows, with the head you chose above. Each strip has 64 numbers. The third strip is the two strips multiplied, number by number. Add the 64 products and divide by 8.

7

All 4,096 scores at once: one matrix multiplication

scores = q_turned @ K_turned.transpose(-1, -2) / 8 # [1, 12, 256, 64] @ [1, 12, 64, 4096] = [1, 12, 256, 4096]

Section 6 was one entry of this table. Row r of q (left) times column j of k (top) gives entry (r, j) of the scores. Head 9 shown. Row 164 is marked; its 4,096 entries are the scores of the bird's square against every row it may read.

8

Where does square 164 look?

shares = scores.softmax(dim=-1) # along each row: exp(score) / sum of all 4,096 exp(score)

Softmax turns square 164's 4,096 scores into 4,096 shares that add up to 1. Below, the shares put back onto the 16 frames they belong to: darker = more. The black box marks the bird in each real frame. Choose the head and the pass.

9

The mix: square 164 takes a weighted sum of v rows

o = shares @ V # square 164, one head: 4,096 shares × 4,096 v rows of 64 = 64 numbers

This is how the past gets in. Square 164's new 64 numbers are the v rows it read, each multiplied by its share. The 6 biggest shares, for the head chosen above (draw pass 1):

o, this head[64]

The v table of head 9, with the 4,096 rows it is read from:

10

12 heads side by side, then gate, add, MLP

o = o.transpose(1, 2).reshape(1, 1, 256, 768) # the 12 heads of 64 side by side again x = x + g1 * block.proj(o) # mix the heads, gate, ADD to the input x = x + g2 * block.mlp(block.n2(x) * (1 + sc2) + sh2) # each row alone: 768 → 3,072 → 768, gate, ADD

11

What leaves block 8?

The same shape that came in, 256 × 768, goes on to block 9. Block 8 also hands back this frame's own k and v, [1, 12, 256, 64] each. In a draw pass they are thrown away: the shelf stays at 3,840 rows.

12

Pass 2, then the push

The picture after pass 1 is half noise. Pass 2 runs the same 16 blocks at noise 0.5 and gives the finished frame. Then the push runs them a third time on that frame with noise 0.05, and this time block 8's own k and v are kept. The shelf would now hold 16 frames, so the oldest, 311, drops off.

13

The window slides: every frame's number drops by 1

Before the push, frame 325 was position 14. After it, the shelf is 312 … 326, so frame 325 is position 13. The stored k of frame 325 does not change (it is plain). Only the turn, made fresh in every pass, uses the new number.

The frame it drew

Model: our stage-3 model, the same weights as the notebook. Every number on this page comes from one run on real frames 311–326. The hand-written block 8 was checked against big.blocks[8] (largest difference ) and the drawn frame against the repo's Streamer (largest difference ).
